whole_original_adopted_publication_confi.description: One fixed two-row symmetric ideal chain has periodic weak and strong Lefschetz behavior in positive characteristic, with a classification over every field extension.
whole_original_adopted_publication_confi.abstract: For each fixed field of positive characteristic p, we construct a single compatible symmetric chain of Artinian ideals in two rows of variables, generated from width three. At every width n ≥ 2, its quotient has both the weak and strong Lefschetz properties exactly when p ∤ n − 1. The quadratic quotient is free over the integers, and a determinant for an arbitrary linear form gives the classification over every field extension. In particular, over the fixed infinite field 𝔽ₚ(t) both properties hold and fail at unbounded widths. This gives a negative answer to the unrestricted eventual dichotomies posed by Römer. It gives no negative answer in characteristic zero or in one row.
plain_language: The weak Lefschetz property asks whether multiplication by one linear form has the largest possible rank between consecutive graded pieces of an Artinian algebra. The strong property asks for the same behavior for every positive power of that one form.

This note gives a single symmetric family whose answer keeps changing as its width grows. Over a field of positive characteristic p, the obstruction recurs whenever n − 1 is divisible by p. The field and the defining rule stay fixed throughout the family.
result: Fix any field K. For width n ≥ 1, let Rₙ = K[x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ] and 𝔪ₙ = (x₁,…,xₙ,y₁,…,yₙ). Define the homogeneous ideal
Iₙ = 𝔪ₙ³ + (xᵢxⱼ : i ≠ j) + (yᵢyⱼ : 1 ≤ i,j ≤ n) + (xᵢyᵢ : 1 ≤ i ≤ n) + (xᵢyⱼ − xᵢyₖ : i,j,k pairwise distinct).

Here 𝔪ₙ³ includes every cubic monomial, including repeated variables; an empty index condition contributes no generators. The quotient Aₙ = Rₙ/Iₙ is Artinian. Every injection of column sets respects the ideals, so the chain is compatible with simultaneous column permutations in both rows. For every n ≥ 3, Iₙ = (Sym(n)I₃)Rₙ: the entire chain is generated from width three.

For every field K and every n ≥ 2, the Hilbert function is (1,2n,2n), and Aₙ has SLP if and only if it has WLP if and only if (n − 1)1_K ≠ 0. The same classification holds after every field extension, including extensions of finite fields. Width one is a separate case: its Hilbert function is (1,2,1), and it has SLP.

For each prime p, work over the single fixed infinite field K = 𝔽ₚ(t). Among n ≥ 2, exactly the widths n ≡ 1 (mod p) are bad. In particular, both properties hold at n = 2 + kp for every k ≥ 0, and both fail at n = 1 + kp for every k ≥ 1. Both sequences are unbounded. This disproves the unrestricted eventual alternatives in Römer’s question for one fixed field and one fixed two-row chain.
why_it_works: The quadratic quotient is already free over the integers. For n ≥ 2 it has degree-two basis uᵢ = [xᵢ²] and vᵢ = [xᵢyⱼ], where any j ≠ i gives the same vᵢ. For each fixed i, the relations identify these mixed terms without introducing torsion, so this basis survives base change to every field.

For an arbitrary linear form ℓ = Σᵢ(aᵢxᵢ + bᵢyᵢ), multiplication from degree one to degree two has determinant (−1)ⁿ⁻¹(n − 1)∏ᵢaᵢ². At a bad width this vanishes for every choice of coefficients, not just for a symmetric test form. Independently, the nonzero degree-one element Σⱼyⱼ is then killed by every linear form.

At a good width, ℓ = x₁ + ⋯ + xₙ gives an invertible middle-degree map. Its square is Σᵢuᵢ ≠ 0, including in characteristic two. These maps cover all powers with nonzero source and target needed for SLP. The proof uses standard integral linear algebra, rank, determinant and socle methods; the contribution is this explicit chain and its complete classification.
limitations: The counterexample uses two rows in fixed positive characteristic. In characteristic zero this particular construction has SLP at every width. It gives no negative answer for arbitrary characteristic-zero chains or for the one-row variant. The width-one exception must not be folded into the n ≥ 2 congruence rule.

The universal written proof establishes the infinite-width and all-field statements. The archive’s finite exact computations supplement that proof. Neither those computations nor bounded literature checks certify exclusive firstness, exhaustive novelty or the present worldwide open status of other variants.
background: Tim Römer’s original contribution, “Asymptotic properties of invariant chains,” fixes an arbitrary field and an arbitrary fixed number of rows c ≥ 1. Its Artinian-chain question asks whether WLP or SLP eventually always holds or eventually always fails. That contribution is on printed pages 1594–1596 of Oberwolfach Report 31/2020. The separate working-group discussion on pages 1544–1545 focuses on one-row monomial ideals; it is a different scope.

Alexandra Seceleanu and Liana Şega’s “General symmetric ideals,” arXiv:2506.15459v1, gives positive results for general symmetric ideals in one row. Its Theorem B assumes an infinite field of characteristic zero or characteristic greater than n, positive integers d,r, and n ≥ max{d + 1, 1 + (1/r)Σᵢ₌₀ᵈ⁻¹P(i)}, where P(i) is the number of integer partitions of i. Under these hypotheses a general (r,d)-symmetric ideal has WLP. Its chain Theorem 9.2, summarized in Theorem C, assumes characteristic zero, positive d,r with r ≤ P(d), a general starting ideal at a width m sufficiently large for Construction 6.8, and n ≥ m. These hypotheses differ from the fixed-positive-characteristic two-row chain here. The v1 arXiv header is dated 18 June 2025; the PDF’s internal date is 19 June 2025.

David Cook II’s work provides standard background on characteristic-sensitive Lefschetz properties. None of these external theorems is needed in this note’s self-contained proof. The earlier project proof in PR1337 is unpublished. The Oberwolfach DOI identifies the original question; this preprint’s solution DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.23570763.

An integral torsion-free basis and the determinant for an arbitrary linear form prove the classification over every field extension. Width one is separately strong Lefschetz. Over the single infinite field F_p(t), good and bad widths are both unbounded, disproving both unrestricted eventual dichotomies in Tim Römer's OWR31/2020 question.

This is a short explicit construction and elementary verification. There is no negative conclusion for the characteristic-zero or one-row variants, no new general determinant or Lefschetz mechanism, and no exclusive-firstness, exhaustive novelty, or present-openness claim. whole_original_adopted_publication_confi.title: An elementary counterexample to a Nullstellensatz for finite-type link invariants
whole_original_adopted_publication_confi.description: An explicit principal ideal in the ordinary finite-order link-invariant algebra has a nonempty actual-link zero set whose vanishing ideal strictly exceeds its radical.
plain_language: A link invariant assigns a number to a collection of intertwined circles. Finite-type invariants form an algebra: they can be added and multiplied. One can ask whether knowing which actual links make an ideal vanish determines that ideal up to taking powers, as in a Nullstellensatz.

This note gives an explicit negative answer to the arbitrary-ideal, actual-link formulation. Its ideal has plenty of actual zeros, including the unlink, yet an invariant vanishing on all those zeros has no positive power in the ideal. The distinction comes from an algebra character that no actual link realizes; it does not contradict the classical Hilbert Nullstellensatz.
result: For every integer m≥2, let X_m be the oriented, unordered m-component links in S³, including split links. Let V_m be their ordinary, uncompleted unital complex algebra of finite-type invariants, with pointwise operations. Order at most d means that the positive-minus-negative crossing extension vanishes on every link with d+1 double points. Each invariant has some finite order; there is no common order cutoff on the whole algebra and no completion by infinite-order series.

For an ideal A, Z_act(A) means its common zero set among actual links, and J_act(S) means all invariants vanishing on S. The radical rad(A) consists of invariants that have a positive power in A. The always-valid containment is rad(A)⊆J_act(Z_act(A)).

Theorem 1. Set g(L)=Σ_{i<j}lk(L_i,L_j)², f=g(4g−1), and A=fV_m. Then Z_act(A) is exactly the nonempty set of algebraically split links: every pairwise linking number is zero. Moreover g∈J_act(Z_act(A)) but g∉rad(A), so the containment is strict. The unlink belongs to the zero set.

The same construction works in the algebra V on all finite-component links, where each invariant has one finite order valid across that whole domain. The finite-type orders are at most two for g and four for f, uniformly in the number of components. The global argument restricts each such invariant to one fixed-component family; it does not assume that every fixed-component invariant extends to all links.

The construction also works for ordered or labelled links, after forgetting orientations by pullback, and over every characteristic-zero coefficient field. The linking-square expression is unchanged by component permutations or orientation reversals. Its actual integer values are considered before embedding into the coefficient field; no ordering of that field is assumed.

The proof companion also records the integer-valued ring version: restriction gives rational Newton polynomials and a ring homomorphism V_Z→Q, yielding the same obstruction. This is not an arbitrary coefficient-ring or positive-characteristic assertion.
why_it_works: On a crossing-resolution cube, an order-d finite-type invariant has a multilinear representative of degree at most d. Products of orders d and e therefore have order at most d+e. Each pairwise linking number is affine on such a cube, so g has order at most two and f has order at most four.

For an actual link, g is a nonnegative integer, being a sum of squares of integer linking numbers. Thus g(4g−1)=0 exactly when g=0, which is exactly when every pairwise linking number vanishes. These are actual integer linking numbers, not arbitrary complex coordinates. Because the algebra contains the unit and A is generated by f, zeros of f are precisely the common zeros of A.

Let L_n, for every integer n≥0, be the coherently oriented closure of the two-strand braid σ^(2n), with m−2 split unknots added. It has m components and g(L_n)=n². Changing a designated crossing in each added two-crossing block either retains that full twist or cancels the block. The resulting signed resolution cube is the forward difference Δ^r[v(L_n)]. This is a crossing-change argument, not smoothing; every resolution keeps the same component count.

If v has order at most d, then Δ^(d+1)[v(L_n)]=0 for every n≥0. Newton's difference formula gives a unique polynomial P_v(t) of degree at most d agreeing with v(L_n) at all nonnegative integers. Agreement on infinitely many integers shows P_(uv)=P_uP_v and preserves sums and the unit. This constructs a homomorphism on the entire finite-order algebra, rather than assuming a character on C[g] extends to a larger ring.

Evaluate that polynomial formally at one half: χ(v)=P_v(1/2). This is a character on the whole algebra, with χ(g)=1/4 and χ(f)=0. For every N≥1 and every finite-order multiplier h, an equation g^N=fh would imply 4^(−N)=0, which is impossible in characteristic zero. Thus no positive power of g lies in A. The proof has no upper bound on N or on the order of h.

The same contradiction can be read as polynomial divisibility: t^(2N) cannot equal t²(4t²−1)P_h(t), because evaluation at t=1/2 makes the right side zero and the left side nonzero. The finite-order polynomial argument proves the universal statement; the accompanying exact-rational checks support its formulas and conventions.

Formal evaluation at one half is not evaluation on an actual link, including the one-component closure of σ. Actual-link values of g are integers, whereas this character gives 1/4. The counterexample concerns using actual links as the available evaluation points; it is not a failure of the classical Hilbert Nullstellensatz on its usual algebraic spectrum.
limitations: The principal ideal A=fV_m is different from the ideal generated by all indexed pairwise linking numbers. That indexed ideal belongs to the ordered or labelled theory, where individual component pairs are distinguished. In that theory the two ideals have the same actual zero set, but g already belongs to the indexed linking-number ideal, so this witness does not decide its radical/vanishing-ideal question.
Algebraically split means that all pairwise linking numbers vanish. It does not mean that the link is geometrically split. The theorem includes split links and does not impose a non-split hypothesis.

No conclusion about completed invariant algebras, homogeneous-ideal variants, positive characteristic, or a knot-only counterexample is asserted. With only one component, g is identically zero, so the displayed witness does not give a knot-only result. Replacing actual links by all algebra characters would change the question.

Polynomiality along twist and braid families is established prior work. The contribution recorded here is its elementary application to the explicit principal ideal and nonempty actual-link zero set. Historical firstness, independent discovery, an exhaustive absence of predecessors and present worldwide openness are not established.
background: Bar-Natan's Problem 2.27, recorded by Ohtsuki on printed page 422, asks the arbitrary-ideal question using actual links as zeros. The collection has volume year 2002 and was published in 2004. Its separate indexed linking-number example remains distinct from the principal-ideal counterexample here.

The polynomiality input is classical. Stanford–Trapp's Theorem E treats full-twist differences; Eisermann develops finite-type polynomiality and the Newton interpretation. Stoimenow's 2010 Theorem 2.1 and Definitions 2.2–2.3 provide an earlier braid-sequence interface and explicitly credit earlier braiding-sequence work. No new polynomiality method is claimed.

Stoimenow's theorem is read with its local odd-exponent and default non-split conventions. One fixed crossing together with local exponent 2n−1 gives even total exponent 2n. The manuscript's direct singular-link argument independently handles the stated full-twist family and all split components. Jeong–Park's connected-sum polynomiality is a related older route, not silently identified with a varying-linking family.

The source comparison supports these specific classical interfaces, including the exact 2010 theorem and its conventions. It does not certify every earlier or final-version proof, exhaustive literature coverage, or the absence of an earlier equivalent ideal counterexample. These limits do not replace the self-contained all-order proof.

metadata.title: An elementary counterexample to a Nullstellensatz for finite-type link invariants
metadata.description:
We give a principal-ideal counterexample to the arbitrary-ideal actual-link Nullstellensatz in the ordinary uncompleted complex algebra of all finite-order finite-type link invariants. With g the sum of squared pairwise linking numbers and f=g(4g-1), the nonempty common zero set is the algebraically split links, but g does not lie in the radical of fV. A character on the entire algebra is obtained by formal evaluation of the standard twist-restriction polynomial at one half. The result applies for every fixed component count m at least two and for all finite-component links; the source's separate indexed linking-number ideal in the labelled theory is not decided.

This is an elementary application of older polynomiality, explicitly credited to Stanford-Trapp, Eisermann and Stoimenow. A bounded primary-source audit found no explicit equivalent earlier counterexample in the inspected bodies, without claiming historical firstness, a new polynomiality method, or guaranteed novelty. The included audit discloses uninspected final-version/body limits. The deposit includes the self-contained research note, LaTeX source and exact-rational verification materials.

AI tools were used extensively in developing, drafting, auditing and adversarially checking the result. This preprint is unrefereed and has not undergone conventional human peer review.
